extra.message: The debug_toolbar middleware is always included in MIDDLEWARE_CLASSES, and the show_toolbar callback (lines 180-185) allows ANY user to enable the debug toolbar by passing 'debug' as a GET parameter, POST parameter, or cookie. This exposes extensive application internals including SQL queries, settings, cache contents, request details, and template context variables without any authentication.
Django DEBUG is set to True, which enables detailed error pages that leak sensitive application internals including settings, database schema, source code snippets, and environment variables.

TEMPLATE_DEBUG is set to DEBUG which is True. When enabled, Django templates will display detailed error information including the full template source, the line where the error occurred, and the template context variables (which may include sensitive data).

The Django SECRET_KEY is hardcoded in plaintext in the settings.py file. This key is used for cryptographic operations including session signing, CSRF token generation, and password reset tokens. Hardcoding it in source control means anyone with repository access has the key, and it cannot be rotated without a code change.

The Django SECRET_KEY is hardcoded as 'h++jszpm)i@p%ay_b=cp#()^od!qns14)h%@qm3)p=cuo+st^a' directly in the settings file. This key is used for cryptographic signing of session cookies, CSRF tokens, password reset tokens, and any data signed with django.core.signing. If this key is exposed (e.g., in public repositories), an attacker can forge session cookies, CSRF tokens, and all signed data.
The CSRF middleware ('django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware') is commented out in MIDDLEWARE_CLASSES, disabling all Cross-Site Request Forgery protection across the entire application.

The X-Frame-Options middleware ('django.middleware.clickjacking.XFrameOptionsMiddleware') is commented out, leaving the application vulnerable to clickjacking attacks where an attacker can embed the application in an iframe.

The X-Frame-Options middleware (XFrameOptionsMiddleware) is commented out, disabling clickjacking protection. This allows an attacker to embed the application's pages in an iframe on a malicious site and trick users into clicking on UI elements. Combined with the disabled CSRF protection, this significantly increases risk.

The Django Debug Toolbar middleware is included in MIDDLEWARE_CLASSES. Combined with the custom show_toolbar function (lines 180-185) that allows enabling the toolbar via debug=true in GET/POST parameters or cookies, this exposes extensive application internals including SQL queries, settings, request details, and templates to anyone.

The session cookie configuration does not set SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=True. Django defaults SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE to False, meaning session cookies will be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections, making them vulnerable to network-based interception by attackers on the same network.

The show_toolbar function allows ANY user (authenticated or not) to enable the Django Debug Toolbar by adding ?debug=1 to any URL, or by sending debug in POST data or cookies. The toolbar exposes SQL queries with parameters, settings, request data, session data, headers, and template context.

The `show_toolbar` function checks request GET/POST parameters or cookies for a 'debug' value and returns True if present, enabling the Django Debug Toolbar for any visitor. This exposes extensive debug information including SQL queries, settings, request data, templates, and cache contents to unauthenticated users. Additionally, the DebugToolbarMiddleware is already active in MIDDLEWARE_CLASSES.

The show_toolbar function checks request.COOKIES.get('debug'), request.GET.get('debug'), and request.POST.get('debug') to determine whether to display the Django Debug Toolbar. Cookies and URL parameters are fully client-controlled — any attacker can set a 'debug' cookie to enable the debug toolbar. The debug toolbar exposes ORM queries, settings, templates, request variables, and other sensitive application internals.

The minified version of the Foundation tooltips library contains the same vulnerability as in `foundation.tooltips.js`. The minified `create` function reads the `title` attribute and processes it through `$('
').html(...).html()` which treats it as HTML content. This HTML is then interpolated unescaped into the tooltip template via `tipTemplate`. When the tooltip element is appended to `body`, any injected HTML elements with event handlers (like ``) will execute JavaScript. The minified code at lines 188-190 shows: `create:function(t){var n=e(this.settings.tipTemplate(this.selector(t),e("
").html(t.attr("title")).html()))...`

The `set_active_from_hash` function reads `window.location.hash.substring(1)` (user-controlled URL fragment) and directly concatenates it into a jQuery selector string at line 142 without any sanitization or encoding. The code does: `.find('.content[data-slug="' + hash + '"]')`. An attacker can craft a URL with a malicious hash fragment that breaks out of the attribute selector syntax, potentially causing unexpected selector behavior or, in older jQuery/Sizzle versions, DOM-based XSS.

The set_active_from_hash function at line 142 directly interpolates window.location.hash (obtained from line 132) into a jQuery selector string without any sanitization: section.find('.content[data-slug="' + hash + '"]'). The hash is attacker-controlled via the URL. An attacker can craft a URL like #foo" onmouseover="alert(1) to inject arbitrary HTML attributes into the jQuery selector context, leading to DOM-based XSS when jQuery processes the selector string.

The tipTemplate function builds HTML by directly concatenating the selector value (which can come from user-controlled data-tooltip or data-selector attributes) into an HTML attribute value without escaping. A double-quote in the selector could break out of the data-selector attribute and inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript. The content parameter is also rendered unsanitized after being HTML-decoded via $('<div>').html($target.attr('title')).html().

The getTip function at line 82 constructs a jQuery selector by directly interpolating the return value of this.selector($target) without quotes: $('span[data-selector=' + selector + ']' + this.settings.tooltipClass). The selector() function (line 88-98) returns the element's id attribute or its data-tooltip/data-selector attribute value. If an attacker can control any of these attributes (e.g., via a stored XSS vector that injects into HTML attributes), the unquoted interpolation allows breaking out of the attribute selector and crafting a malicious jQuery selector or even executing code in older jQuery versions.

The create function at line 100-101 retrieves the title attribute value via $target.attr('title') and passes it through $('
').html(...).html() — a jQuery roundtrip that converts HTML entities to actual HTML — then injects this into the tipTemplate HTML. The tipTemplate function (line 15-18) concatenates this content directly into a tag: '' + content + ''. If the title attribute contains HTML with event handlers (e.g., ), these will execute when the resulting HTML is appended to the DOM at line 104 ($tip.appendTo('body')).

At line 19, the template directly assigns the global variable `solutionHTML` to the innerHTML property of a DOM element: $('div.solution')[0].innerHTML = solutionHTML. This is a classic DOM XSS sink. The variable `solutionHTML` is not defined or sanitized within this template — it is expected to be populated by the including page's JavaScript or by server-rendered data. If `solutionHTML` contains any user-controlled or unsanitized data (e.g., from a backend template context variable serialized as JSON), arbitrary HTML/JavaScript execution is possible.

The `{{qs|safe}}` expression on line 48 injects user-controlled query string data into a JavaScript context without escaping. The `|safe` filter disables Django's auto-escaping, and since this is inside a `<script>` tag (`var x = "{{qs|safe}}";`), an attacker can break out of the string context and execute arbitrary JavaScript.

The `{{qs|safe}}` expression on line 28 injects user-controlled query string data into an HTML attribute value (`value="{{qs|safe}}"`) without escaping. The `|safe` filter disables Django's auto-escaping, allowing an attacker to break out of the attribute and inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript.

The `{{path|safe}}` expression on line 49 injects user-controlled URL path data into a JavaScript context without escaping. The `|safe` filter disables Django's auto-escaping, and since this is inside a `<script>` tag (`var myvar = "{{path|safe}}";`), an attacker can break out of the string context and execute arbitrary JavaScript.

The `{{qs|safe}}` expression on line 37 injects user-controlled query string data into a JavaScript context without escaping. The `|safe` filter disables Django's auto-escaping, and since this is inside a `<script>` tag (`var myvar = "{{qs|safe}}";`), an attacker can break out of the string context and execute arbitrary JavaScript.

The user_pic view takes a filename from the 'p' query parameter without proper sanitization and joins it with the base path to read and return the file contents. An attacker can use '..' sequences to traverse the filesystem and read arbitrary files (e.g., ../settings.py, /etc/passwd). The error messages even guide the attacker by distinguishing between '/' and '..' attempts.

The user_pic view reads a file from the filesystem using a filename taken directly from the 'p' query parameter without adequate sanitization. While os.path.join is used, if the filename starts with '/', os.path.join ignores the base_path and treats it as an absolute path. Additionally, '..' sequences allow directory traversal. The error messages at lines 44-49 even hint at path traversal techniques (starting with '/' or '..').

The user_pic() view function's error handling (lines 44-51) reveals specific information about the attacker's path traversal payload to help them refine their exploit. The function checks if the filename starts with '/' or '..' and returns different messages accordingly: 'That was worth trying, but won't always work' for absolute paths, 'You're on the right track...' for relative path traversal. This actively assists an attacker in crafting the correct path traversal payload.

The user_pic view has a denylist check for path traversal sequences ('/' and '..') but it only runs AFTER the file open attempt fails (in the except IOError block). This means the check is purely informational and provides no actual protection - the path traversal already occurred. Additionally, the check is incomplete (only checks startswith('/') and startswith('..')), which can be bypassed with encodings or alternative traversal patterns like '....//' or '../..//'.

The user input submitted via the 'first_name' POST field is not validated or sanitized before being base64-decoded and passed to exec(). There are no restrictions on what code can be executed, no allowlist of safe operations, and no sandboxing.

The code_execution view takes user input from the 'first_name' POST parameter, base64-decodes it, and passes it directly to Python's exec() function. This allows arbitrary Python code execution on the server. The Python 3 branch at line 72 uses bytes() and base64.decodestring().

The code_execution view takes user input from the 'first_name' POST parameter, base64-decodes it, and passes it directly to Python's exec() function. This is the Python 2 compatibility branch that executes if the Python 3 branch fails.

The xss_form() view sets a cookie with key 'monster' and a session-like value, but does not specify HttpOnly, Secure, or SameSite attributes. Without HttpOnly, the cookie is accessible via JavaScript, making it stealable via XSS. Without Secure, it can be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections.

The users dictionary at lines 115-126 hardcodes user data including email addresses (PII) directly in the source code. While this exercise data is intended for educational purposes, embedding personal information in source code is a poor practice that can lead to information exposure through version control history, backup files, or source code leaks.

The dor_user_profile view takes a userid from the URL path and accesses/modifies the corresponding user profile without any authentication or authorization checks. There is no logged-in user concept, no session validation, and no ownership verification. Any user can view or modify any other user's profile by simply changing the userid in the URL. Additionally, the 'admin' flag in the user data (line 124) can be modified through the POST handler at lines 133-134, allowing privilege escalation.

The dor_user_profile view performs no authorization checks when users access or modify profiles. There is no verification that the requesting user owns the target profile, allowing unauthorized access to all user profiles.

The boom() view raises a generic Exception with no error handling. If DEBUG=True in Django settings, this will display a detailed debug page with stack traces, settings, environment variables, and source code context.

The missing_access_control view allows any user to access the admin page by passing ?action=admin without any authentication or authorization check. There is no session validation, login requirement, or permission check.

The missing_access_control view renders an admin page when action=admin is passed as a query parameter, with no authentication or authorization check whatsoever. Any unauthenticated user can access the admin interface by simply adding ?action=admin to the URL.

The `csrf_image` view is decorated with `@csrf_exempt`, which disables Django's Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) protection middleware for this endpoint. This allows an attacker to craft requests that execute state-changing operations on behalf of an authenticated victim without their consent.
The 'url' GET parameter is passed directly to Django's redirect() function with no validation of the URL scheme, domain, or path. Any URL, including javascript: URLs or file: URLs, can be supplied.

The `unvalidated_redirect` function takes a `url` parameter from user input and passes it directly to Django's `redirect()` function without any validation. This allows an attacker to redirect users to arbitrary external websites.

The `unvalidated_forward` function takes a `fwd` parameter from user input and uses it to look up and call any function in the module's `globals()` dictionary. This allows an attacker to invoke arbitrary functions defined in views.py, including `admin`, `sql`, `code_execution`, `user_pic`, and others by simply passing their names as the `fwd` parameter.

The 'fwd' GET parameter is used to look up a function name from globals() and then call it with the request object. This allows an attacker to invoke ANY function in the module's global scope, bypassing all access controls. Functions like admin(), code_execution(), or even private helpers can be called directly.

The unvalidated_forward view takes a function name from the 'fwd' query parameter and looks it up in the module's globals() dictionary, then calls the resulting function with the request object. This allows an attacker to invoke arbitrary view functions, bypassing intended access controls. For example, passing 'fwd=admin' calls the admin function, 'fwd=boom' triggers an exception, 'fwd=code_execution' triggers code execution.

The unvalidated_forward() function takes a function name from the 'fwd' query parameter, looks it up in the module's globals(), and calls it with the request object. This allows an attacker to call any function defined in the views module, including admin() to access the admin page, boom() to trigger exceptions, or other views with unintended parameters.
